She is sorry the Father is going to the country and cannot help her. She should accept the girl as agreed. She is pleased with the girls' behaviour; she should encourage them to pray for providence. On the spiritual path one cannot always be fervent: Jesus alternates sweetness and dryness.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have your letter and hear what you say about that person; he will certainly have been [struck] and suffered not a little. I am sorry he is going to the country, because he won't be able to help you.1

2. As for the girl, I tell you to take her; the terms you set are fine.2 In such matters you must be decisive and act on your own, since they are already settled; I urge cleanliness.

3. I am pleased with the girls; tell them to pray so that providence may soon reach you, and then they will go on an outing to the country.

4. You say you feel cold.3 We cannot always be fervent, because that is how our Jesus deals with his Brides: today a little sweet, tomorrow dryness and sadness. St Teresa said she was very glad in times of dryness because she knew her Jesus was preparing a sweet for her; but in times of sweetness she trembled, because she knew bitterness would follow.

5. The enclosed letter is for that person; keep it, and he will send for it. I close, or it will miss the post. Listen, my dear, be sure to take back everything you sent to Gigino; for pity's sake, the silver! My God! My God! Be careful that nothing gets lost.4

I am your affectionate MOTHER ROSA

The sister should go home to her family as agreed: her native air will restore her health. She should be more self-reliant: commend herself to God and go forward with courage. The Mother will return to Piacenza after the girls' examinations. She should entrust Sr. A. Paola with directing the embroidery work.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have just received a telegram from you; I don't know how you can have forgotten what we agreed over so many days: that if this sister's parents came and wanted her home, you would hand her over to them, pointing out that her native air would do her good and she could recover her health.1 I am not replying by telegram because it seems pointless, and besides I cannot tell you all this by wire.

2. I think you should pay a little attention and remember what I arranged before leaving; then these things would not happen.

3. I have just received your letter and heard all you say.2 God will see to it himself if the Marchioness will not. My dear daughter, try to be more self-reliant, otherwise it will be as with Sr. A. Elena and we shall always be the victims.3 Does that mean Sr. A. Eufemia is better?4

4. In some cases you must decide for yourself: first commend yourself to God, then go forward with courage.

5. I hope the examinations will be on Thursday and that I shall be back on Saturday, God willing, or next Monday at the latest; I hope you have received my letter with one inside for that person.5

6. Listen, if any fine work comes in, put Sr. A. Paola in the school to direct it; then little by little we will leave her there, because I think that is her place.6

7. You did very well not to send these letters, and likewise any others that may come to you from others or from her;7 certainly the talk those two indulged in is truly reprehensible, and you must call them and give them a good penance to punish their wicked tongues, for they must not speak of such things, which are none of their business; a religious should not know such things.8 Goodbye; I am dressing to go to the Cardinal.9 I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA. God bless you.

She writes from Ferrara, where she has gone for the pupils' examinations. In a few days she will be back and will leave at once for Nizza to arrange the opening of the school.

A.M.F.

My good Father Agostino,

1. Just a line to ask for news of you; I am anxious because I have been without it for so long. I write in my own hand, and then Sr. A. Vincenza will; now I am writing from Ferrara, where I am for the girls' examinations. The Countess is in Rimini.1

2. How glad I would have been to receive letters from you saying you were coming to Piacenza. I return there on Saturday and from there go to Nizza, where I have been called about the schools they want to open in October.

3. If you see Father Angelini, greet him for me; I don't write to him for fear of being a nuisance.2

4. I won't speak of my health and troubles, for it would take a ream of paper.3 God the Father's will be done; there is an abyss of them on every side.

Bless me; I hope to tell you more in person.

Your poor Sr. A. M. ROSA GATTORNO

She should face every setback with courage and faith, and have more prayers said for providence. Advice on dealing with the girls and with some Sisters. She will be back in two days.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. After dinner I received your long letter, which I read with pleasure. You answered Signor Defilippi admirably; before consulting anyone, this indelicate, affected sister should have asked me.1 How it makes one's blood boil! My daughter, for pity's sake, don't lose heart, don't fall ill, take things from God's hand; He will give us all we need.

2. When the novenas the Father mentioned are finished, begin one to St Joseph for providence, and tell the girls to pray fervently. Make it privately, without benediction of course; if he then sends you providence, you will give it.2

3. Listen, say these words of mine to Sr. A. Paola: "The Mother charges me, by her order, to put you in the school with the older girls". And take out Sr. A. Pia, who can then serve you as nurse.3

4. You ask what penance to give those who dirtied the wall. Three a day, in the refectory, kneeling, they will say: "Sister, I have been disobedient; pray to the Lord for me". That means there are six, three at a time, and then a good scolding.4

5. I hear all you tell me about that person; was there a battle? From your words it seems so.5

6. Has Cristina gone? I hope you sent her; so on Saturday I shall be with you on the 6 p.m. train.6 I enclose two lines for Alessandro; if he is no longer in Piacenza, forward them.

7. I am most displeased with Sr. A. Eufemia's conduct. I would be inclined not to cross Defilippi, but let him act, and then we will do what has to be done in due course; tomorrow we have the examinations and then I am free.7

8. What grief the lack of providence causes me! When will that Person return from the country? Did he tell you?8

Goodbye; my head is spinning; it is late.

I am your affectionate MOTHER ROSA. God bless you.

She approves what was said to a Priest. She is sorry about the girl sent away from the school because she could not pay; she herself would have kept her, trusting in providence. It is best to keep silent with the person causing trouble and to pray for her. Suffering smooths our way to heaven. She should look after her health; she will come to Piacenza to rest a little. News of the sisters in Genoa.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today I received your letter;1 I hear what you say about Mgr Ma. You answered everything well; be of good heart; you also did well to tell Don Ronco; and you were right to think it better for the priest first to speak to Mgr Mariano; so go to him and talk to him about it, for I have already written him something this evening. Tomorrow or the day after I will write to Mgr Giordani.

2. I would have kept that poor girl who left because she could no longer pay; God would have seen to it. You will say: "It's all very well for the Mother to talk, always the same, but meanwhile I'm the one here". God alone sees and knows what pain I feel: a knife piercing my breast.2

3. You did well always to keep silent with N.ta; you will see her turn will come soon; He who guides and governs the Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, is above all.3 He will set everything right; I pray for her and for all who cause these troubles and sorrows, sure that you will do the same; and in this way we are sure of treading the safe path that leads us to the kingdom of Heaven.4

4. Blessed are the afflicted, for they shall possess it; so all sorrows, all torments open the way for us to arrive there happily; a short suffering for an eternal joy! What happiness, my beloved daughter; for the love of God everything is too little.5

5. Last night, unable to sleep though it was late when I went to bed, I did nothing but pray for the Countess; I said to St Francis our father: "Go, my Father, go, give peace to her heart; bind her to the Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, with your holy cord".6

6. My dear, one thing I urge on you: take care of yourself and your health so that you can work in God's work; and with your health as the excuse you will come down here; meanwhile be sure to instruct Sr. A. Domenica well in everything. What is Sr. A. Apanasia doing, the silly thing? How well Sr. A. Eletta is doing — it's a joy; if you saw her you would be amazed. Just now when I need a Superior exactly like her, silly Apanasia, how she wastes herself!7 The Superior, Sr. A. Serafina, is better. Perhaps tomorrow she will begin to get up.8

7. As for the uniform, do what you can, provided it is ash-grey; buy the cloth, make sure it is ash-grey.9 You asked about buying a dress for Maddalena; listen, soon we shall have the clothing of many postulants and then I will send you one; indeed, you can take one when you come.10

Goodbye, for it is late and I can do no more. I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA. The Lord bless you and everyone.

She asks the Mother to write; very well, she will give her some small corrections. On her last visit the Mother was displeased by: her complaining in a loud voice; her not accepting poverty; her wanting to hide the house's poverty from the Sisters. She would be glad to see her more steadfast in virtue, attentive and aware of her task as Superior. She is to read the Sisters the exhortation to poverty that the Mother should have given in person. She ends by inviting them to pray to obtain from God the Father, through the intercession of her friend Rosa Parodi, who died with a reputation for holiness, providence and the gift of practising and loving poverty.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today I received another half-sheet. You ask me to write to you; what should I say? That if I offer any correction you will take it badly and make scenes, as I saw you do in my presence when I tried to correct you. A thousand ailments come over you. How it displeased me to see you ever more irritable and above all raising your voice till it shrieked; I found this fault in you worse than before; it tore my soul: "they're all interested in whether I have [money] or not!". Listen, it was you who made it loudly heard. And then your agitation; it is right that the sisters need not know you have no money, and that is good; but to hide that we are poor!2

2. Listen, I will confide something to you: having agreed to this myself left me with such pain that it torments me still, and I shall not be rid of it until you have read these two lines to the Sisters. I hope you will.3

3. How glad I would be to see you a little more steadfast, faithful in your office and particularly in anything that could give scandal, such as going to sleep together with Camilla. Daughter, believe me, a Superior must keep a certain decorum, a certain propriety of person, such as [avoiding] sitting on the floor or being all unlaced; you may be unlaced in the same way, but with a little more modesty.

4. Think when you have to speak; in short, the composure your position requires; and then you will see that when the sisters hear your voice and are corrected, they will amend.

5. I want you to take these warnings of mine with resignation, not as a reproach but as advice.4

6. Watch the cooks so they do not waste; in short, be all eyes.

7. Here are the two lines:

My daughters, you know well how dear poverty is to this Mother of yours. She loves it, embraces it and always clasps it to her breast; but alas! my soul is wounded by you on this account,5 because I see that you love it little and, to put it better, do not know it.

8. Listen, I cannot find words to make you know its exquisiteness; I will only tell you that it is the treasure of the Saints. Yes, we are poor and we rejoice in it. Ah! If I heard the Daughters of Saint Anne say so, how happy I would be! But quite the contrary: they want nothing to do with it.

9. My God! what sorrow; well then, the Holy Mother forces you to embrace it, and indeed in your house there is far less providence than in all the others, do you understand? So pray.

10. Listen, I had a friend who is now dead; her name was Rosa Parodi; she died with a reputation as a saint, and I have already obtained many graces through her.6 Make a novena to her that she may send you, that is, obtain for you from God the Father providence and with it the gift of practising poverty and loving it; that she may obtain for you a taste for this treasure; and meanwhile promise God that, with his divine help, you will practise it.

11. Pray to her from the heart and you will see that you will have providence, for I tell you that you need it; not riches, but I would like you not to have to run into debt.

12. These things I tell you so confidingly I would not want any of you to be so thoughtless as to start talking about with others, not only outsiders but not even among yourselves, building castles in the air and wanting to say things or make comments. If anyone dared do so, God will mark her!

13. Instead you may encourage one another to pray to this dear holy soul and ask her for providence. I tell you your house needs it. So make a novena all together with fervour; pray and you will see that you will obtain everything. Goodbye; the Lord bless you always; believe me your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

Notices about two postulants. She should get the money for a payment. Firm measures are needed for one sister.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have received yours about the postulant Adelaide's money. Have them write that it should be brought, that is, brought to the postulant herself. I let you know that a postulant will come from the Sacro Monte of Varallo; accept her; she will bring something.1

2. Go to Brigidini to see if he has the 700 F.; if he has, take them at once to Merli.2 I had someone write again but he gave me no answer; I know the Marchioness will (?); patience is needed; these are terrible times; God alone can sustain us, and this He does and will do.3

3. My [dear], try to put an end to the quarrels. Listen, when we can get Sr. A. Fortunata on her feet, I want her to go home, without fail; she is too bad; she is not worthy to die a Daughter of Saint Anne.4 In haste, I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

4. The Superior has got up and is well; I will bring her with me to

Piacenza.5 Goodbye, but there will be time; I think it is far off… [the time of return].

She encloses a letter for the Father. She suggests what seems right to say to a Sister. She should have prayers said for the Father and for the Superior in Genoa.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Just a line to enclose this one for that person.2 Get it to him at once; even if it cannot be put into his own hands, no matter: let the porter give it.

2. Give Maddalena a thousand greetings: she is not to confess the community's sins but her own; she must not go to confession twice in one day but only once; and then whatever God inspires you to say.3

3. Today you gave me no news of that [person]; write at once how he is; I hope you have had prayers said; I am anxious.

4. The Superior here has relapsed and is not very well;

say a few more prayers, that God may heal her again.4

I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

5. I go to bed saying to the Lord: bless my daughter and give her strength to carry the whole enormous weight she has on her shoulders.

She writes, taking advantage of a little time. She should ask Signor Squarzoni whether it is true that the Countess will no longer give any subsidy. They manage to earn by their work, so she should look for work, visiting various friaries. She should keep an eye on the kitchen sisters. The Mother has everything needed for the altar and will send it all when the work in the Chapel is finished.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I don't know how you can be so upset that I don't write; you know well that my head no longer allows me to be so busy. Immense were the sorrows and troubles of these days, which gave me no rest; now, although I have toothache, I am answering you, having a little time.

2. Listen, send for Signor Squarzoni and say to him: "Do me the kindness of relieving me of a great worry: people say the Countess no longer gives us anything. Is it true?" And stop there; say nothing more.1

3. But don't worry, for I know he is due to bring it to you in these days; it is just his way. Enough; do this at once; it is not that this good gentleman is unwilling, but he has immense worries.2

4. Now to Sr. A. Apanasia. If she cries, take her to Piacenza and tell her firmly that you are sending her away.3

5. You see, my daughter, that work is providence, as this poor mother of yours told you. Send to the Dominican friars, the Carmelites, in short to everyone; seek and you shall find; go to that old Capuchin who came once and promised me he would speak to some devout person; commend yourself to him, he is so good; you'll see he won't make you feel at all awkward and you'll be glad. You must go yourself, not the others.4

6. I also urge you to watch over those two in the kitchen; I have a thought constantly in my mind that worries me about them.

7. Listen, the candlesticks have arrived from S. P. d'Arena with everything needed for an altar; they are magnificent, but I won't send them until you have the altars and it is finished.5 As for Squarzoni, do at once what I write, and then do your duty by the Countess.6 I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

Greet everyone for me. God bless you; every day I never fail to commend you in a special way.

She shares her grief and the Sisters' at the Superior's illness. She urges her to let herself be guided by the Superior with docility and trust and to imitate her virtues.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have received your letter and am glad to hear that the Sisters are all well; but believe me, the grief you feel for your good Superior is no less mine. Pray, pray; God can do all things; press upon His heart and He will restore your Superior to health.2

2. My daughter, I urge you to economize and to keep accounts carefully; but I would not want you to take what I say as meaning you should make the Sisters suffer, for pity's sake; on the contrary, get them everything they need.

3. I urge you, for charity's sake, to be all eyes for the good running of the house and observance, and see that silence is kept; in short, try to imitate your Superior's virtues in docility, and be careful in sending Sisters out to beg.

4. In short, manage as you have done so far; be very careful in assigning the nurses; and then, listen, when you go to your Superior,3 tell her everything frankly and learn from her how you should proceed.

5. Do not let yourself be taken over by that ugly spirit of vainglory, but let humility be your guide and always try to act with it; you will see that one day the Lord will make you happy on earth as in heaven.

I am your affectionate MOTHER ROSA

Greet everyone for me, and may God the Father bless you and pour out on you his choicest blessings.

10 September 1872.

Countess Caracciolo has visited her; Sr. A. Vincenza forgot to warn her beforehand. A Priest from Ferrara has told the Mother that the Sisters are not called to nurse the sick because not all of them do it well. She is grieved and prescribes that Sr. A. Giovanna give them a lesson every day. Various advice about the house and her conduct towards the Countess.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I hope you have received my letter; I hear that Countess Caracciolo came.1 It is true that I had promised her to let you know, and I told Sr. A. Vincenza. She forgot to mention it when writing to you.

2. Listen, a Priest from Ferrara came here and said that the reason you have no patients is that people were not satisfied with the nursing you gave and that some sisters do not do it well. Some do well, others not. What sorrow I felt! Let them know it.

3. I want them to have a lesson every day; if they don't know where to hold it, let it be in the parlour, and the teacher will be Sr. A. Giovanna; tell them so.2 How painful these things are, and still more to think that if they reach the Countess's ears — how dreadful, my God, what things she will say!

4. I beg you not to run up accounts, for charity's sake;3 mind, I repeat, it is the small expenses that steal large sums.

5. Listen, I ought to tell the Countess that the Saint Anne is there provisionally, but that the Countess will soon send her own, and we will take that one back to Piacenza.4 For charity's sake, with the money you receive, think that it will be better to buy plenty of flour after you have paid the baker.

6. Recommend that girl from the theatre to Mgr Mariano, otherwise she will be lost; let her go herself and plead; you make it clear that your needs are such that you cannot admit her with nothing.

7. Again I commend the sick to you; see that you watch over this and get the reports every day; go yourself.

8. Listen, when the Countess comes, show her the register of the day school,5 so she will see how many girls have been admitted and how many have already gone into employment. Show her everything properly, the good that is being done. If she said she could treat them to an outing in the country,6 then you will take your boarders too; but for charity's sake don't let slip a single word, however small, that might suggest you have such a wish. As for the Ursulines, you did well not to go to the celebration, but I hope you went afterwards to pay them a visit.7 I close because I am going to the Morte. I am your affectionate. Greet everyone; I will soon write to Camilla.8

I am your affectionate M. R.

She is to give the enclosed letter to the sister and see that she is not influenced by Sr. A. Panasia. It is all right for the girls to have singing lessons from a master, but only as an exception, to honour the Countess. She should check the nursing of the sick personally. The Mother will go to Nizza.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today I received a letter from you and hear of the long visit you paid to the Ursulines.1

2. Give this enclosed letter of mine to Sr. A. Camilla; keep an eye on her so that she does not go about with Sr. A. Apanasia.2 How much worry that mad, proud head of a sister gives me, truly possessed by some spirit that is not good. Enough; the Holy Mother will act and somehow be rid of her, and will not let her do anything that could [be] harmful to her Work.3

3. As for singing, when they have sung the little song to the Countess, stop it at once and tell her: For our dear Countess4 every exception is made, but otherwise our Institute cannot allow this instruction, since they are poor girls, and we would only be feeding their longing for the theatre and such things.

4. I commend the sick to you; try to visit, pay them a visit.5 I have not yet received the smock.6 On Monday, God willing, I leave for Nizza, where I shall stay a little, and then for Genoa, at S. P. d'Arena. I am overwhelmed; read it as best you can and believe me yours for ever

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

As for the girl, do as you said; if she doesn't pay, send her to us. God bless you.

She advises her to press Squarzoni to take an interest in the work on the house. News of the health of the Superior Serafina and of her own; she urges her to take care of herself. She gives the names of the sisters who have died. Fr Tornatore is in Siena and will then go to Foligno, where we too are about to open a house.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have just received a letter from you with much news, good and bad. I hear about Squarzoni; what can I say? She writes me so many things, and meanwhile the building work has stopped; I gather it will be finished — by St Linus — the feast of the Moorish Kings; what grieves me most is the money. Patience; go there often so that he will remember; and he also has the clock to give you.1

2. In your other letter you told me about Sr. A. Camilla; listen, everything you did, you did well, my dear daughter.2

3. Have prayers said for the Superior Serafina, who has been seized by a very high fever; I am tied down here like a dog and for the good of the Work cannot move.3 Take care of yourself, I urge you; mind, if one overdoes it, one no longer knows what to do. Yesterday, as usual, after much suffering, I received at 11 at night a telegram saying she was ill. I leave you [to imagine] what a night I had; I was seized by convulsions, though I felt utterly resigned and, I would say, numb. Yet seeing myself tied, unable to fly to her,

my heart was wrung, and that was all. My health too is going downhill at a gallop.

4. The sister who died is Sr. A. Elena; the other (two) are: Sr. Anna Eufemia, and the other Sr. A. Fortunata, Sr. A. Raffaele. My dear, so many dead; they grieve me!4

5. At the Morte the Superior, who is doing so well, is Sr. A. Filippina; she does so much good, I am pleased with her.5 It is true, the Father left 8 days ago for Siena to give the retreat to the Sisters of Charity and then goes to Foligno, where, in all confidence I tell you, we shall soon open a [house].6 Silence, for charity's sake! Goodbye, my dear daughter. God bless you, and believe me ever your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

Greet everyone for me. I am delighted to hear that you are being called to nurse the sick.7

She should see to organizing the Spiritual Exercises in the Mother House. The Mother has written to various people for money. Three postulants will arrive. Once the deed dividing Sr. A. Emilia's property is obtained, she should charge the Parish Priest with selling her share; it can be offered to her brothers.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. You will receive this by Sr. A. Giacomina.2 It would be good for you to tell Signor Defilippi3 that if you could get a missionary, the Vice-Superior, or someone else, to come and give the Exercises, then those from the Morte could also attend, teaching only in the morning and then coming straight to the Casa del Verme, beginning on Saturday and so finishing the following Sunday. Do try to have them made.

2. I wrote to the Marchioness, I wrote to Father Cirillo, and also to Brigidini, asking him kindly to provide you with 700 F. and something more to give the miller and Condiviola, and that these should be the lottery money, if he would be so good as to hurry it along.4

3. You will see that instead of 4 the postulants are three, all young. My dear, the one I thought would give me 500 F. gave me nothing, and this was a muddle. I will tell you about it in person. The other two gave me something, but now I await

Brigidini's answer; if need be I will put them together and send them to you; I hope he will do it.5

4. You cannot imagine my distress when I think of my Sr. A. Serafina.6 My God, I don't even know where my brain is, so many and so great are the cares and sorrows of every kind.

5. You ask me about Buon Pastore. Listen, I think the best place would be the Morte, because there she could receive Communion more often than in this house.7 As sacristan you can put Sr. A. Giacomina, should she fall ill; otherwise say nothing to her.8

6. The postulant you will see is the most ladylike is from Acqui; try to keep her; treat her like the others, only she seems to me a little more melancholy and not very robust; I would like her to stay because there are weighty reasons.9

7. See that all make the Exercises, since they have few patients. You should go early to St Lazarus to beg the Superior and the Procurator; beg and entreat them. I think it is the only way to get anything.

8. Sr. A. Serafina seems a little better. You will talk to the Parish Priest of Settima: as soon as you have the papers he should try to sell; he can offer it to her brothers.10 Sr. A. Giacomina will tell you about Sr. A. Eufemia.11

9. Send three ducks at once to Don Accinelli; I'll send you the address; how much he did for the Sister! Do everything to obtain Sr. A. Emilia's deed of division, so that you can also borrow money on this land, speaking with the Secretary. In short, I have put the water on the fire, and I hope to come out of it well.12

10. On Monday at 6 a.m. I leave for Genoa; write to me there.13 As soon as you can get a turkey, send it [to] Accinelli; don't buy it, but do everything to get it as alms.

I am your affectionate MOTHER ROSA

She urges her not to overtire herself. She tells her that a sister and three postulants will arrive. She encourages her to hope in providence.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Two lines in haste. My dear Franceschina, for charity's sake don't wear yourself out, for you see what grief it is when you are ill!

2. You have done everything well. Listen, on Saturday the Superior will arrive with three postulants; put her to sleep upstairs like the others, call her Sr. A. Giacomina, not Superior, and then I will write you another letter on how to proceed.1

3. I have written to Brigidini, to Father Cirillo, to the Marchioness Anguissola and also to Sr. A. Pia;2 tell her that I will write to her, the Superior of the Morte.3 Believe me, my dear daughter, I haven't a moment to breathe; I am smothered with work. Trust in God; everything will come, you'll see.4 Be of good heart.

I am your affectionate Mother. God bless you. Ever your

MOTHER ROSA

She feels for the needs of the house. She could tell Squarzoni that she truly needs the money. Courage; God will reward her for everything. On the Mother's return she will call her to Piacenza. In a few days she leaves for Genoa. She should ask Squarzoni for the money to pay the Priest and try to have Mass in the Institute, at least on Sundays.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have just received your letter; I hear what you say about the sisters and Squarzoni. It would be [good] if you could say a word to Squarzoni and tell him you are truly in need.1 Courage, my daughter; God will reward you for everything, and when I return to Piacenza I want you to come to Piacenza and spend a few days there.

2. Meanwhile have prayers said for the Sup. A. Serafina, that she may soon recover; I am on thorns because I cannot move from here until next Monday; I will leave by the 6 p.m. train and arrive in Genoa at midnight.2

3. Write to me in Genoa; tell Giovanna not to get notions into her head but to pray, so that she may soon have the hospital. Today it was discussed at length, but nothing was settled; tell her to pray.3

4. You can tell Squarzoni that the Priest wants to be paid — he doesn't say so, but I am ashamed — and if he will kindly give me the money I will pay him;4 and then go to the Capuchins and look for a Mass at least for feast days, and then providence will provide; commend yourself; and if you have to be without for a while, you have the church nearby on Sundays; in short, you must keep looking until you find a Priest who will say it free. I write no more because I am in a hurry. Goodbye; I am yours. The Lord bless you all, and you in particular.

[MOTHER ROSA]

Suggestions for the house. She should send ten manuals of Saint Anne. The Mother has done what she could to obtain help. She should have prayers said for the health of the Superior in Genoa.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have just received yours; I hear what you say about providence, the Priests who came, and so many things.1

2. Listen, I want you to have Sr. A. Giacomina work as house nurse, and then send her to the sick.2 Then I would like you to send ten (10) manuals of Saint Anne to Canon Quaso;3 put in with them a box of chalk for writing on the blackboard; I enclose the address.

3. Sr. A. Paola should be at recreation with the postulants.4 I commend to you the nursing school. I need a nursing sister and don't know whom to choose.

4. I wrote to Father Cirillo,5 and also to the Marchioness and to Brigidini. I await a reply. I begged him for charity's sake to give the 700 F. and something for Cordivialo too, for I am in extreme need. I leave nothing undone.6

5. I thought I would get something from the postulants, and they will all give it a little at a time, including the one you put downstairs; no one; it would have [been] better to put her with the others, but what you did is done; don't change it for now and then we shall see.7

6. Listen, have prayers said, for charity's sake, that God may heal the Superior in Genoa for me. Goodbye; I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

God bless you and everyone.

She must bear daily sorrows with courage. She may give up the wardrobe requested and try to arrange the Sisters' belongings on boards laid on the floor of a room. She should get ready to go to Piacenza for a while; the Mother will go to Ferrara only when the work is finished, for the thanksgiving celebration.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Just a line to tell you that you must be strong; I feel your sorrows and they all sink into my soul; I would like to relieve you of them by taking everything on myself, but, my dear daughter, know that after suffering and pain you will find consolation in the very sorrows you now endure.1

2. Courage, my dear, and you will see that good Jesus will come to console you; alas, we know that men have nothing for us but crosses and sorrows.2

3. She wants the wardrobe;3 give it to her and put your things in a room; spread sacks and boards on the floor and then lock that room; if they say: "What have you got in there?" — "Our wardrobe, since we haven't a wooden one", and laughing: "How happy we are! Like this in everything". Then, as for Mass, try to get rid of this expense; go to Mgr Giordani, beg him and see that he says yes.

That expense is too much. Let us leave it to the Lord and you will see that He will set everything right.4

4. Meanwhile get ready, for when I go to Piacenza I absolutely want you to come with me for a while, because I certainly shall not come to Ferrara again until the Te Deum is sung, and that will be after Easter.5

5. You see, my dear, who knows, perhaps going to Foligno will actually be arranged.6 Sr. A. Serafina is a little better; from the consultation held on Friday it seems she can be cured.7 Goodbye for now; write to me in Genoa, where tomorrow, God willing, I shall be at 11 p.m. Greet everyone for me; I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA. God bless you.

She recommends that Sr. A. Giacomina be made to work. She should let the Mother know when the Father returns to Piacenza.1

1. I tell you to make Sr. A. Giacomina work; that way she will make up for all the idleness of these months.2

2. When that person arrives, write to me; I don't know where to write; if you know, tell me. When he comes, write to me; meanwhile I will send you a letter; keep it with you and give it to him when he comes.3

Goodbye, I am your

affectionate [MOTHER ROSA]

She wants to know whether a triduum was celebrated for a deceased lady. She charges her with sending the Countess the salami she had had prepared for her.1

A.M.F.

[My daughter]

1. I want to know whether you held the triduum for Signora Biale that I told you to hold, with Mass and Miserere, benediction, Requiem Mass, in short a triduum, because Don Biale went to the Delegate in Genoa and asked for it; this evening I am having the Priest himself write to him that everything he ordered was done.2

2. If they iron the albs, they should not starch them, because then they are no good for putting on the lace; we will see to it when I come.3

3. Send that little cured sausage without pepper that I had made for the Countess.4 If it is too long, divide it, then wrap it well and send it to her with a covering letter that Sr. A. Vincenza will send you in draft this evening; have it copied out fair and then send it. It should be a little longer than a span.

Goodbye, I am your

[MOTHER ROSA]

She should treat the two Sisters who will arrive firmly, see that they work and take part with the others in the Spiritual Exercises. The Mother is anxious about the scarcity of providence. For charity's sake she should take care of her health.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. You will receive this by Sr. A. Prassede. See to putting her on the latrines, and if she says she feels ill, tell her that all the sick go to the House of the Morte; and so to Ludovina; and say this to them: "I warn you that the first time I receive a report about you and that you have said anything about the other house, that is,

the ones you came from, there will be no other way out for you than to take off your veil, and you will be sent away at once without mercy".2

2. See that they work, and they will make the Exercises, then all those who also all, and the postulants too; but never stop sending them to the sick.

3. If you have not yet sent the books with the chalk, add a book of the Exercises, you know, Father Manfredini's.3

4. Send me, well secured, the Deed of the Polleri bequest. It is in the tin box in the cupboard; put it in another envelope and, with five seals, send it to me.4

5. How much grief I must feel about providence!5

Today I accepted a postulant with 500 F. She is from the Sacro Monte of Varallo. She will come to Piacenza; if she lacks anything, accept her, being... then I will tell you everything in person. As long as she doesn't do as those from Nizza did, all the 500 F., and then! my God! what grief!6

6. Give this letter of mine to that person as soon as he comes, which I think will be tomorrow.7

7. At this [moment] I have decided to leave these two with her, because I hate having to spend 24 F. on these constant journeys. How it makes one's blood boil!8

8. I hear from a letter of yours that I received a few hours ago that you have been spitting blood again.9 For charity's sake, I don't know what to say if you all fall ill! Take care of yourself, don't overtire yourself, for you know it is overwork and bile that make you ill. I add no more; I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA. God bless you and everyone.

She asks her to send what she requested. Some notices. The sister had asked her something, but the Mother cannot remember what: she is too taken up with so many thoughts, worries and sorrows.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Yesterday we arrived safely in Nizza, accompanied only by a bad headache. I hope to be in your arms on Saturday; meanwhile I would like you to send me what the enclosed note lists, and Sr. A. Elisabetta's overcoat.1

2. Meanwhile I would like you to send the picture of Saint Anne to Don Accinelli, Priest at S. Lorenzo, to his home, Cloister of S. Lorenzo.2

3. I write no more because I am unwell; the tickets are working splendidly; I have not seen the Priest from Ovada; the young postulant you mention, put her in the kitchen for Sr. A. Nazzarena to teach her, under the cook Giovannina; so she will learn, and then I will send her to Genoa.3

4. I remember that in one letter you asked me something, but my head can no longer tell what, and it would take me too long to go through them all.

5. The overcoats for those in Genoa will be sorted out; send only Sr. A. Elisabetta's; I don't know how it is that the teacher has not yet come. Enough; we will see to everything when I come.

Goodbye; greet everyone for me, and believe me your affectionate MOTHER ROSA

6. P.S. I have just received all your letters. My dear daughter, I am worn out and half dead. So many troubles stifle me and take my life away; I can bear no more.4 Goodbye; I am yours, living and dead.

She sends a letter of exhortation for the sick sisters so that they may know how to suffer in a spirit of penance. She cannot say exactly when she will leave.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Don't trouble yourself over this letter; I will tell you everything in person. Listen, my daughter, it would be good if you read it to them yourself: how the bed of sickness should serve to purge our many faults so that we may be spared Purgatory; instead we pile fault upon fault and end up having to undergo a long and painful purgatory.1

2. My God! Have pity on me. I won't tell you where I am going, because I cannot; perhaps it may even be today, and when I go I will telegraph you, because I don't know when it will be.2 Goodbye; I am in a hurry, having much to do; all for God, all for Jesus,3 always, for ever and ever.

Once more your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA. I would like to know how that person is.4

She learns with the greatest displeasure of the sick Sisters' demands about food. They are to keep to the rule she made. She is to read them what the Mother writes. On her return the Mother will go to them.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I hear with the greatest displeasure of the cravings of the greedy invalids; this I cannot, will not tolerate. What? Puddings, etc.? Am I to be an instrument of damnation for these thoughtless women by giving them what they want?2

2. Well then, before leaving I remember that I made a rule, and I want it read (to them) and kept.3

3. We are poor; they must practise poverty; so I command, so the Holy Mother wills.

4. How dreadful! Are the Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, all to die with the sin of gluttonous intemperance?4

5. My hand trembles; I cannot even go on; read this letter of mine aloud to those thoughtless women.

6. What constant grief this causes me. From now on I shall not be indulgent but severe, austere as never before. At least on my part, at God's tribunal I shall have nothing to condemn me. I think I give the example; they see how long5 these four bones have been ill and are still infirm — and do they need puddings and are never satisfied?

7. Journeys, sorrows, torments; a potato boiled in water, a plain soup — I find in it all the flavours in the world.

8. In short, let this be the last time I hear the sick speak this language; I have had enough; I want to hear no more.

9. I want you to go at once to the Morte and read this letter of mine. I don't know if you will be able to make it out, but the grief, the anguish, the pain they all make me feel now forces me to act like this.

10. Take courage; if you don't want to read it yourself, give it to the Superior, who by virtue of obedience is to read it to them at once.6 And don't go to that house any more;7 I will go when I arrive, though I don't know when that will be, since I may have to leave again for somewhere else;8 it might even be today.

I am your affectionate MOTHER ROSA

Advice on running the house. She commends the poor and the sick to her. She encourages her and the sisters to accept suffering lovingly for God's Work.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have just received a letter from you (1). I see, my dear, that you did not understand properly about the stamps; it was not the one on the outside that was old,1 but there were so many old ones inside the letter; it was pointless to put them in. That's how it is, do you understand? It's nothing; don't give it a thought.

2. Listen, tomorrow you will receive a postulant; Don Accinelli has already been told by telegram. He will send her to Piacenza with your sister, and he will take the money, being already in charge of everything.2

3. Listen, my dear daughter, you are not to give anything to the Superior at S. P. d'Arena. Do as I told you, and I hear you are doing so; give everything to Don Accinelli; that is right. Keep a little for petty expenses, and for the rest carry on as you are doing, for I am pleased.3

4. Now another thing. For charity's sake, don't forget to care for the poor. I am so sorry that the woman you write about died without the sister there. Do what you can to satisfy them.4

5. Listen, consult Accinelli, and if I need to send more sisters I will send them at once. I am having a postulant trained for the kitchen; so when she is clothed I will send her to you.5

6. Send your letters to me in Piacenza, for tomorrow at 10 I shall be there, God willing. Pray for me, because my health is very bad.

7. I commend the sick to you: satisfy them as much as you can and proceed as I told you.6 Always go forward with strength; God will help you, while I bless you together with all my daughters.

8. Courage, for God's work is great, and great must be its sufferings. Blessed are you who share in them; so one day we shall be in that blessed dwelling which none enter but those who knew how to carry the cross with Jesus.7

Goodbye in the heart of this God who is all love; I leave you, but I always hold you close, calling myself your affectionate Mother Rosa.

Read these two lines to everyone at recreation. I am your

affectionate MOTHER ROSA

She requests an annual grant for the Institute at Sampierdarena, a well-established work for the benefit of the townspeople and the care of the sick.

Most Illustrious Mayor and Distinguished Councillors,

1. The undersigned, driven by the need in which this poor house finds itself, earnestly begs your Illustrious Lordships to deign to listen to what the petitioner humbly sets forth.

2. This poor House is in the utmost need, having, as your Illustrious Lordships well know, a very considerable number of girls, all poor, from this town, and also a large number of nurses who daily devote themselves to caring for the sick.

3. I would need more of them to be able to meet the requests, but unless I am helped by your Illustrious Lordships, it is impossible for me to continue so well-established a Work.

4. So that so useful and beneficial a work may not fail, I beg your Illustrious Lordships to take this charitable Institute into consideration by granting it an annual allowance, in order to settle a debt incurred for the maintenance of the girls and to meet future expenses.

5. I therefore place my trust in your Illustrious Lordships as the only support for continuing well a work so well begun.

Confident of obtaining everything, I thank your Illustrious Lordships in advance, and sign myself your Illustrious Lordships'

Most devoted Servant Sr. A. M. R. GATTORNO

She is sorry the Father is unwell; she should get the enclosed letter to him. Various notices and advice. She should send a copy of the "faculties for our Chapels".

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I am extremely sorry to hear the Father is ill; keep me informed of his health.1 I am sending you this letter; send it to him at once, at once; let it be handed even to the porter if the Father cannot be seen, but at once.

2. My dear daughter, if you think of sending Sr. Adelaide to Nizza instead of Luigia, for fear of her eyes, do as you think best, but she must be quite cured.2

3. I hear what you say about the Morte. Listen, tell the Parish Priest that Sr. A. Maddalena is going to see whether the air would do her good, because I fear she may end up like the other one; but that the teacher is coming and he will be pleased.3

4. Listen, the one from Lodi will come after All Saints, so she writes. I don't know what to say; you will see everything will [be settled]; I hope to come soon. Manage the Morte as best you can; when I come everything will be put right. I commend the schools to you, for charity's sake: don't let them fall behind.4 In haste, I am your

Affectionate M. ROSA

OtO

5. P.S. Send me the copy of the faculties we have for our Chapels.5 Listen, it is in a large envelope together with the others in Don Luigi's hand; it is the last one we received and still to be copied;6 have it copied, and [of] those where it says Communion, funerals and holy oils are granted, send me the copy, not the original. The copy is enough, at once, for I need it; so there must be two: one in Don Luigi's hand and the other you will have recopied.

See that this letter reaches its destination at once, at once, for charity's sake.

She asks for a letter of recommendation to the Prefect of Alessandria in order to obtain from the State Property Office some rooms of the former Benedictine nuns' convent.1

Your Excellency,

1. The kindness and charity with which you deigned to receive me whenever, in my need, I came knocking at the door of your noble heart, encourage me now to turn again to Your Excellency, not knowing to whom better to address myself in hope of being heard.2

2. I therefore beg you kindly to send me here in Genoa, where I am, a few lines of recommendation to the Prefect of Alessandria, so that he may deign to say a word to the State Property Office to expedite the matter of a building, formerly a Benedictine convent, to which is attached the small Hospital occupied by the poor Daughters of Saint Anne, who are too cramped;3 that is why they are asking the State Property Office for the outbuildings of the Benedictine Convent.

3. I will go to Alessandria myself to hand him your esteemed letter, being, as on other occasions, [sure] of obtaining what I desire, supported by your most noble words. Forgive the liberty I dare to take, confident of your indulgence.

Please present my respectful greetings to your most honourable Wife, while I have the honour to sign myself your

Most humble Sr. ANNA MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

She is sorry to hear the Father is unwell and sends a letter for him. The scarcity of providence is a serious matter in Genoa too. The Superior Serafina is better, but other sisters are ill.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have just received yours, having come back from papa's. From this last one I hear news of that person, which is never as good as I would wish, always much the same.2 I enclose two lines for you to send him; but I had written a letter to Alessandro with one inside for that person. I hear he could not give it to him. Patience! Everything goes like that for us.

2. You speak to me of providence; here too it is a serious matter. Patience; so the Lord wills. Let us hope and trust; we shall have everything.

3. The Superior: the doctor [said] this morning that now there is nothing but weakness; the illness is cured. Thank you for the prayers you had said.

4. I won't go on, because if you saw it, it is a real hospital: Sr. A. Vincenza has a cough and is in bed, Sr. A. Serafina is in bed, Carlotta is vomiting; in short, I no longer know what to say or do. May God have mercy on me. Tribulations without equal. What sorrow, what anguish! Upstairs there are two more who are ill. I hear what you tell me about Brigidini.3 [As for] Pestri, do whatever God inspires you.4 I am your

Affectionate M. R.

It is impossible to write every day: Sr. A. Vincenza is ill and the Mother has so much work inside and out. She is negotiating for a new house and planning several journeys; the sister should get her the reduced-fare railway tickets. She will receive a quantity of soap. Courage; providence will come.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have just received your letter; I am glad to hear that person has recovered.1 Blessed be God! Just two lines to tell you that you would like a letter every day, and for us it is impossible: Sr. A. Vincenza is always ill. For several days she has been in bed with a bad cough, so I have to do everything myself: write, go out. In fact yesterday I came home soaked through. I had to go and see a house which I have finally secured; it is very fine.2

2. Carlotta has been vomiting and this morning does not feel too well. Tomorrow I go to S. P. d'Arena and then, if the railways are finished, that is, repaired, I will go to Nizza. For now, if it keeps raining, it will be a serious matter to move at all.

3. Meanwhile, please be so kind as to go to the railway Director, that is, the station, to learn how to get tickets, and then ask for two for Nizza, two for Piacenza, and two days after that I would need some for Ferrara.3 Find out how it is done; here I don't know whom to ask.

4. You will receive 50 kilos of soap; I found it so [cheap] — it comes to 44 cents a kilo by the piece. You must cut it into small pieces and then leave it to dry.

5. Don't worry about providence; you will see it will come; patience is needed; as long as this [wretch] lives, you will always have to suffer like this.4 There is great poverty everywhere.

6. I enclose a note for Alessandro; I would like to know what he has done with my letter that he was to take to that person; if he has not yet taken it, get it from him and deliver it when you are quite sure it will reach him in person.5

Goodbye; greet everyone for me, and believe me your

Affectionate M. R.

7. P.S. Send for news of Brigidini's wife every day.6

She has already begun some negotiations about the hospital the sister wrote of. She should get the tickets as requested. The Superior is getting worse. If she thinks fit, she may arrange the clothing of the postulants once they have made the Spiritual Exercises and informed their relatives.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have just received yours. 1st: I will tell you that this Hospital you mention was discussed in Nizza, and I had almost settled everything with a priest who is a member of the Congregation.1

2. Good; so get me the tickets:2 three for Nizza, and then ask for three more for Ferrara. I leave on Monday the 28th for Nizza. The travellers' names are: Sr. Rosa, Sr. Vincenza and Carlotta, if she can pass as a postulant, as she may be said to be. I shall be at Novi at 9.37;3 I will stay 8 days in Nizza, and if I have to go to that place, provided it is arranged, I will go.4

3. The news of the Superior today is very bad, and I fear she will not recover.5 I will send for the pills; meanwhile I tell you to look after yourself. Carlotta is better; Sr. A. Vincenza is well. For charity's sake, look after yourself. Tell Father Paolo that I have as many Religious as he wants and that I had already discussed this matter at length with a Priest. So I think I have explained myself very well.6

4. Then I must leave again as soon as I reach Piacenza.7

Today it is pouring and at noon I have to go to the

Mayor of S. P. d'Arena.

Goodbye, I am yours; greet the sisters for me.

5. If you think of clothing all the postulants, you may do so; I would be glad, so that we could make use of them. The one with 250 F. in her trunk, the one from Acqui, should send for it. Then with a hundred Fr. or so you can clothe them all. You could have them make the exercises with Defilippi and then clothe them; think it over and do as you think best.

6. That taramaj who looks after the pigs,8 you will wait for a while longer, so she can become a little more refined. If you decide on this, they should all write to their relatives on the day they are clothed.9

7. Send me the railway tickets as I wrote in my other letter.10

Goodbye; the Lord bless you. I am your

Affectionate M. ROSA

She is glad of the news of the house. Sr. A. Vincenza is not very well; Sr. A. Serafina is seriously ill again. She should try to avoid the expense of Mass, and if the Countess wants it celebrated later she should be satisfied, and likewise be free to take whatever she wishes.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have received yours and hear of the work you are doing for our great benefactress; indeed, she has had someone write to me that she wants everything made and sewn by you and the little girls.1 I am glad to hear you have been able to pay the bills. If only I could say the same!!...2

2. I am in a hurry, because Sr. A. Vincenza does not feel very well, so I am writing myself. Sr. A. Serafina makes us fear again because of her relapse.

3. As for Mass, I think I told you: get rid of this expense.3 The Countess would like Mass said later; tell her you will always be content, even if it were said at noon. Let her take whatever plates she wants and anything she wants.4

4. I shall not be able to come before the third or fourth, and I am still doubtful whether I can. Today I have a fever and am badly worn out. Anguish is not lacking. Blessed be God!

Greet everyone for me, and believe me your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

Sr. A. Serafina has received Viaticum; she edifies everyone. She asks for information needed for the work at Nizza.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Viaticum has just gone out for poor Sr. A. Serafina. Her resignation is indescribable. She looked like a St Teresa, always smiling; she is a mirror of virtue; here there are no cravings;2 the Dominican Father edified. I write to you with tears in my eyes.3 God will not leave her to me; patience!!4

2. Ask Father Paolo to give you the Priest's name, because I spoke with one in Nizza and we had arranged many things; he was, as I told you, on the Commission of this Hospital. Send me the address; I will write to him or send someone, so that we can understand each other better.5 We have the house; it is something fine. I will write soon. I am in a hurry; yours in the depth of sorrow

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

She asks her to buy and send what she has listed.1

1. My daughter, a line to ask you to buy everything on this little list.2 If you can, send it all at once.

2. I am on my feet as God wills. Pray and have others pray, for charity's sake, for this is a time of adversity. As soon as I have a moment I will write to you at length.

Greet everyone for me; God bless you; I am

your poor MOTHER

In reply to his request, she sets out the indispensable conditions she lays down for accepting the nursing of her Religious in hospitals. She is willing to discuss it in person while she is in Nizza.

Reverend Sir,

1. I reply to your esteemed letter, giving you all the explanations Your Reverence asks of me regarding the functions of our Institute and what is required for nursing in hospitals.1

2. If the Hospital calls the Sisters to nurse, the least that can be done for them would be 400 F. each and firewood.2

PRESENTATION

A sound interpreter of the Second Vatican Council and of its directives on the renewal of religious life, Fr Elio Gambari reminds us in his Manuale della Vita Religiosa alla luce del Vaticano II that «fidelity to Founders/Foundresses is one of the fundamental principles of renewal. In its Founder/Foundress the Institute rediscovers itself, its own individuality or identity and its own dynamism» (Ch. X, p. 77).

Now, a good way, perhaps the best among the many possible, of living in fidelity to Founders/Foundresses is to know their writings, their letters, in which they convey to those they address something of themselves: their ideals, their deepest aspirations, their thought, their longing to work tirelessly for the glory of God, the service of the Church and the good of their brothers and sisters.

Aware of this, the Daughters of Saint Anne, in order to remain ever more faithful to their Foundress, are continuing with praiseworthy family spirit the publication of M. Gattorno's letters. In June they presented us with the 2nd volume of the letters written by M. Rosa from 1871 to 1872; today they give us another volume, the 3rd of the series, covering the following two years.

In the letters collected in this 3rd volume M. Gattorno continues to reveal herself, as I noted in presenting the previous one, as a woman of «fascinating and overwhelming human and mystical personality... wife, mother and foundress... rich in the delicately human sense of a St Teresa of Avila and at the same time in the warm mystical inspiration of the great reformer of Carmel».

The letters of this 3rd volume have a distinctive feature that particularly enhances their interest and importance. They were written at one of the high points of the Foundress's life and work: the four years 1871-1874, which the compiler, Sr. Anna Maria E. Convertini, calls the period «of the Family's initial development in the structural shaping of its communities and charitable services, and of M. Rosa's spiritual tension arising from her ardent desire to see the Family inserted into the 'life of the Church' through the approval of the rules».

In this period of the Institute's development and structural shaping M. Rosa had to endure a real martyrdom, often comparable to the sufferings of Jesus from Gethsemane to Calvary. Indeed, in several letters one seems to hear the echo of the existential tension in which

she lived. One example is when, writing to the Cardinal Vicar Costantino Patrizi, she assures him: «There is no anguish, no sorrow, no agony of which my God does not mercifully make me a most generous gift»; and to her dear Daughters: «Let us try, then, to go step by step along his way (Jesus'): to suffer, to toil, to deny ourselves so as to do in everything the will of the Eternal God».

M. Rosa, assisted by God's grace, continued on her way, sure that the Lord would never abandon her, and she was able to pass on to her dearest Daughters her serene fortitude in trial and her unshakeable trust in God's help, as is easily seen in the edifying reading of the letters, from which not only the Daughters of Saint Anne but all who have the chance to read them will learn the Gospel virtues: humility, poverty, patience, diligence, frankness, obedience, fortitude, serenity... all joined to a great love of prayer, love of suffering, desire to be humbled, a spirit of recollection, devotion to Jesus Crucified and to Our Lady, etc.

I congratulate the beloved Daughters of Saint Anne on this new volume of their Mother Foundress's letters, a true gift of God, an authentic present from the Spirit and, I would even say, a precious monument to the holiness lived and achieved by M. Rosa, a true «valiant woman» who was always open to divine grace and lived with constant, loving trust, abandoned like a daughter in God's arms. With the publication of this volume they will have at hand a most useful means of knowing M. Rosa's Gospel spirit in depth and, as I said at the beginning of this presentation, by reading her letters they will come into loving and profound harmony with «her ideals, her aspirations, her thought, her longing to work tirelessly for the glory of God, the service of the Church and the good of her brothers and sisters».

Fr Carlo Lizarraga, C.P.

Postulator of the Cause of Canonization of Mother Rosa Gattorno

INTRODUCTION

This volume completes the body of letters from the four years 1871-1874, which, as was pointed out in Lettere, 2, (p. 18), are marked by a fundamental historical and charismatic unity. The letters of this period express the initial development of the Family in the structural shaping of its communities and charitable services, and the spiritual tension of Mother Rosa arising from her ardent desire to see the Family inserted into the «life and holiness of the Church» through the approval of the Rules — an approval she had thought she would obtain easily and quickly, but which, because of the careful and prudent examination characteristic of the Church's usual criteria, proved difficult and dragged on for years. To her the delay was incomprehensible and not free of interventions hostile to the good: «Instead of fostering God's Work, they put it in chains».

The explosive growth of the Institute

What urgently drives the Mother to seek approval promptly is the awareness that she has acted in God's Work at the express command of the Holy Father Pius IX. «He is the true founder».

True, her clear awareness of the gift of the Spirit is that she has let herself be guided by the Spirit: «I have put everything in God's hands... I want only God's will, and in it I wish to die» (L 93); yet she wants to be confirmed in the path she has taken, she wants God's Work to bear the seal of the Church, so that it may be freed from any constraint that might hinder its growth and prevent it from spreading throughout the world «like the flight of a dove». Was this not the prophecy of her Holy Father Pius IX?

On the other hand she clearly sees the Rules as the genuine and faithful expression of the charism and of her conception of life, as well as the fruit of her experience, and as the indispensable instrument that conveys the spirit and life of the Family to the young women called to belong to it. The Church's «reasonable» delay in approving them is a most painful sorrow to her: «No one can believe how much pain this business causes me, having so many religious to train in this spirit and nothing, neither printed nor handwritten; I beg it of you for pity's sake» (to the Secretary of the S. Congregation of Bishops and Regulars - L 76 -). A sorrow joined to her many physical

7

and moral sufferings: «Without strength, laden with pains from head to foot, plunged in anguish... going step by step along his way

(Jesus'); to suffer, to toil, to deny oneself so as to do in everything the will of the Eternal Father» (L 42).

Humanly she is «a rag», yet she is almost always travelling along «his way». A quick look through the letters in this edition gives us the timetable of her journeys across northern and central Italy to the places where the Daughters of Saint Anne already are or are beginning their presence. «1872 keeps me in chains — she had confided to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa from Ferrara, where she was drawing up the new Rules — but 1873 will not be like that». The dawn of the new year finds her in Genoa, encouraging the Sisters in their annual retreat; she then visits the House at Sampierdarena; on 13 January she sets out for Rome. A brief stop in Piacenza, where Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino is waiting to accompany her; a stay of several days at Foligno for the foundation of a new House. Amid a thousand difficulties, misunderstandings and suspicions (L 9) — «the little devil is already starting to poke his tail in and drive me to despair» (L 11) — and unheard-of physical suffering — «I am so ill that God alone sees what I suffer... I have so many pains that every moment I felt I would faint» (L 12) — she manages to start the new work (cf. Index IV). On the 24th she is in Rome. Without delay she again takes up the problem closest to her heart: the approval of the Rules. Here too troubles and toil await her: «This morning my head is reeling; so many troubles! I feel I am dying. God grant I hold out... here it is again a question of our name (Daughters of Saint Anne); how dreadful! A devil underneath stoking the fire» (L 28).

Meanwhile she has responded positively to the request of the President of the Ovada (AL) hospital (L 17) and hastens to instruct the Superior Francesca Camisa, sending her to accompany the Sisters and stay with them as long as needed to set up and run the hospital service properly. She makes herself present in the other communities by letter, taking an interest in their small and large daily problems, advising the superiors and intervening directly by letter with the local authorities in matters within their competence. Meanwhile in Rome too she is called from many quarters to intervene with her Sisters in situations of pressing need. The Ladies of the «St Monica Catholic Circle» soon manage to offer her the collaboration, however small, she needs to realize what she has desired for years. «I have been given a house here in the holy City, in Rome, to open two day schools and to nurse the poor sick at home» (to Bishop Ranza, Piacenza, - L 44 -). A house: a few bare little rooms placed at her disposal by the Marchioness Maddalena Galleffi, Superior of the Oblates of Tor de' Specchi, next to the Monastery (L 38). Between March and April she starts four communities in Rome, which involves much moving of Sisters and multiplied work for her, amid difficulties and worries. In the same period her presence is also needed at Foligno, and each time a good dose of wormwood is in store for her: «This morning too I have had my fill of spasms, for I had another a few hours ago; enough, for the love of God everything is too little» — including the open, hostile plotting of ill-intentioned hired thugs, and even an attempt to set fire to the house (L 60; 62). Everything is too little for one who loves.

After six months she leaves Rome, but not before going, surrounded by her «Roman» daughters, to the Holy Father to receive, with his blessing, his authoritative word, which gives her confidence for the future of the Work. The journey back is broken first by a stop at Foligno that lasts longer than planned, then at Florence, where she «arranges to accept a house to be opened in August»; at Bologna she accepts two more houses. At last, Piacenza. «I found — she writes to Fr R. Bianchi, who is revising the Rules — half a village: girls, postulants, religious, all in order and at peace, with exact observance» (L 114). As usual, and more so, she is exhausted: «This time the weakness will not leave me; the breathlessness has eased, but my strength is quite gone; I cannot stand at all» (to Fr A. Donadio - L 117 -). Yet she goes on working. «Who is holding me up?» she asks in amazement. Her answer is abandonment, with growing awareness and trust in her dear Eternal Father: «Do, do what you will, my God; I am content and, like a lamb at its mother's breast, I am at peace» (L 99). From the deep peace of this calming immersion in God, ever more drawn into the Work he entrusts to her, her commitment to self-giving grows stronger: «For his Work one must give without stint. He gave all his blood for us and so must we, blood for blood» (L 135); and from her giving «blood for blood» springs the fruitfulness of God's Work. She sees it grow, flower and bear fruit: the Piacenza house is full of religious and postulants (L 180).

The many young women who keep arriving at the Mother House, sent by parish priests and others or drawn to the Family by the witness of Mother Rosa and her daughters, are the shining sign of that fruitfulness, as are the many new houses springing up.

In every call, from wherever or whomever it comes — Bishops, parish priests, priests, presidents of Pious Works or lay people eager to do good — she hears the very voice of God showing her where to go; and every request releases in her the spring of urgent charity.

Nor does she let herself be held back by any practical difficulty, and she dislikes procedural delays. She sets out her conditions for starting a work, so few in truth as to discourage no one: at least four sisters, a «small» dwelling with the bare necessities, a minimal contribution in money (Lett. 17, 48, 98, 127, etc.). A stranger to any trace of earthly interest, she draws her inspiration solely from Gospel criteria and looks to Jesus Christ: «My Saviour! You who preached in the open, without house or roof, had nothing but the glorification of your Father; and we? How it pains me always to hear that to do a little good one needs comforts!» (L 338). «Prudence, yes, but not a prudence like today's, when to do a little charity we religious must be paid over the odds. How dreadful, what an ugly spirit» (L 234).

The GIFT and the gifts

This brief cross-reading of the volume from the standpoint of the Institute's expansion is merely a beginning and is meant as an invitation to continue and go deeper. We conclude it with the language of numbers, incisive and significant in itself. At the beginning of 1873 there were 7 houses, at the end 17; by the end of 1874 there were 24. In 1873, 53 Novices received the habit of the Daughters of Saint Anne; in 1874, 83.

Alongside this theme of the Institute's expansion, significant for its vocational, practical, cultural and historical implications, there are others no less important. First, the many-sided figure of Mother Rosa in the various facets of her personality as woman, religious and foundress, her psychological traits, the lines of her pedagogy as educator of the Daughters of Saint Anne; her relations with various personalities, her friendships; Mother Rosa and the Church, with the related problem of juridical recognition; Father Tornatore and his presence in the Institute; her closest clerical and lay collaborators, etc.

A prolonged, in-depth study «with an understanding born of love» would lead to fruitful discoveries, knowledge and appropriation of the GIFT and the gifts of the Spirit in the persons of M. Rosa and Fr Tornatore, in the life of the Family they brought forth by the Father's will and in the fruitfulness of the Spirit, as a response of distinctive Gospel life in the Church, following the poor Christ.

She has had good reason to withdraw the teacher Sr. A. Carmelina from the school for health reasons, and this causes no harm, since the assistant is standing in. Most Illustrious Sir,

  1. I have a letter from the Superior there telling me that Your Illustrious Lordship visited the school and, finding a qualified teacher missing — Sr. A. Carmelina — said there was a danger the Inspector might complain.1

  2. From my little knowledge I tell you that, since Sr. A. Carmelina teaches the second class and has her assistant, I saw nothing wrong in withdrawing her for a fortnight for her health, and I am sure the Inspector can say nothing.

  3. Meanwhile I inform Your Illustrious Lordship that Sr. A. Carmelina seems to be recovering very well; I shall wait another eight or ten days and, if the convulsions do not return, I will send her back to her post or else replace her with another.

  4. Your Illustrious Lordship had told me, indeed given me your word, that whenever anything arose you would let me know; so I rely on your word with confidence.

  5. I would point out one thing — but I don't want you to think I wish to avoid sending the teacher — not that, for the schools and house of our benefactress, Princess Pallavicini, will always come first and will always be provided with teachers and whatever is needed.

  6. For your guidance only, then: I have opened a school with 161 girls and have only one qualified teacher there; the others are all assistants; the Inspector and the Director visited that school, examined it and gave me a certificate of satisfaction.

  7. Please be so kind as to reply and tell me everything you find amiss in that school. I have received a warning — I tell you in all confidence — that reveals to me certain little things connected with the visit you made with Ghelli.2 But I have laid everything at the feet of my Crucifix; He is my master; may He bring his divine will to fulfilment in us.

Please accept my greetings, and kindly pass them on to your most worthy Wife, while I sign myself Your Illustrious Lordship's

Most humble Sr. Anna M. R. G.

Most Illustrious Inspector,

With all esteem and respect I sign myself Your Illustrious Lordship's

Most humble Sr. Anna M. R. G.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I am very sorry to keep hearing of new troubles, but if God so permits, let us adore his divine will.

  2. I am more than delighted to hear about the nursing of the sick. Ah! these are the ones who do us great good! Try to satisfy them, so that we may become known and the town may appreciate our work. I am also delighted that the Sisters are well.

I am your affectionate Mother Rosa

Most Illustrious Director,

  1. The countless proofs of your exceptional kindness that Your Illustrious Lordship gave me whenever you visited our poor Schools in Piacenza embolden me to ask you a favour for which I shall be most obliged.1

  2. I would therefore like Your Illustrious Lordship to write to the Schools Inspector in Ferrara, describing our way of teaching, whose aim is the good of our neighbour.2

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Pay attention, for charity's sake, and read this carefully. Go with Sr. A. Camilla to the Schools Superintendent and give him this letter.1 For pity's sake, be careful! If he questions you, answer that in a few days the qualified teachers will be back, that meanwhile there is one, and that two will qualify2 next autumn, pointing out Sr. A. Camilla. If he speaks of the boarding school, that is, the girls you have in the house, tell him there are 8, or however many there are; I thought there were 8 and put eight without being sure, but that does not matter.

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Last night I received your half-sheet. I hear all about Fr S. Very well; see that his postulant is happy and grows fond of Saint Anne, and she will stay.1

  1. Tell that person that I have already arranged everything for Sr. A. Ippolita; when I heard she had left, I at once saw to putting things in order for her so that nothing would happen. Tell him also to have you make your vows on Sunday or Monday.5

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

to dispose of the Sisters without the Superiors' permission.3
