In short, explain things well to her, and tell her not to appear anxious but hard-working, so that the town may see in her the active, charitable Daughter, all zeal for her neighbour, receiving the sick in the Hospital with love; so tell her clearly how to proceed, how matters stand between us and the President, that is, the hospital, financially of course; how to act when the Sisters are unwell; in short, for charity's sake, keep her close to you and teach her.4

  1. Enough; now try tactfully to put it right and arrange to call the other two soon; and you, even alone, provided you find good company, can go to Piacenza. As long as you can be in Piacenza at the beginning of next month, since I need Sr. A. Adelaide.6

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughters

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. A line, my dearest ones, to thank you for the constant prayers you offer for me; I tell you I feel their great effect, for I am still on my feet, though I toil immensely, always unwell, and now and then I have to lie down; but after an hour's rest I go back to work.2

  2. Yes, my dearest daughters, let us work tirelessly, for we have an eternity awaiting us in which to rest. Oh! blessed is she who has worked as a true vinedresser in this vast field of nursing the sick, and she who has known how to perfect this work by observing our Rules.3

  3. Courage; good Jesus taught us; let us try, then, to go step by step along his way: to suffer, to toil, to deny ourselves so as to do in everything the will of the Eternal God.

  4. Love, love this Redeemer, and take refuge often in his Heart, until you come to dwell there night and day.4

  5. Pray, especially in this month of my glorious saint St Joseph, that he may obtain for us from the Child Jesus to grow in his divine

love, and for me, wretched as I am, the grace I am asking of him, and the other, which is for our Institute; and providence too. Tell him to send you a bigger house as well, for I am distressed to know you are always so cramped, especially for sleeping.5

  1. Let us hope; St Joseph can obtain everything for you if you pray to him well and keep a fine month for him; for pity's sake don't lessen your prayers for me; and I also want the nursing of the sick, your sufferings in the night watches — I need them so much.6

  2. Who is holding me up? I keep asking myself. Without strength, laden with pains from head to foot, plunged in anguish, I live, one might say, as a corpse that moves; I ask nothing of my God except that his divine will be done in me.

  3. Oh! dear daughters, if good God gave me the strength of a giant and joined to it a proportionate suffering, perhaps this most unworthy mother of yours might barely manage to expiate some of her infamies.

  4. My God, have pity on this last of the Daughters of Saint Anne, who bears the name so unworthily. Pray,7 and I hold you all together — as I do every morning — in the Heart of Jesus, where you may be set aflame with the charity of love.

May the Eternal Father pour out his choicest blessings on you all, while with all affection I remain your

Affectionate Mother Sr. A. M. Rosa Gattorno

  2. I am sure your health will continue good, trusting in God to keep Your Most Reverend Excellency alive for many years, for such are the prayers that rise to God every day.

  3. I have received your esteemed letter and am most grateful.2 I commend to you the poor House of Piacenza, while I implore your Apostolic Blessing and remain with veneration Your Most Reverend Excellency's

Most humble Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

She has been offered some furniture for the house at Tor de' Specchi and asks how to arrange transport.

Your Excellency,

1. Having been offered today some pieces of furniture, which I gladly accepted for the house at Tor de' Specchi that Your Excellency is opening for the benefit of poor humanity, and fearing to trouble you by calling in person, I thought I would humbly send you this note asking how I could have it taken there.1 I await your instructions, while I remain Your Excellency's

Most humble Sr. Anna M. R. G.

She should have the postulants' dormitory tidied and kept ready. She will leave with the Sisters the Father indicates. Courage and see you soon. Leave the keys with him. Bring food for the journey and the money.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I have written to that person about those you are to bring with you. He will tell you exactly what to do; meanwhile I am writing to Genoa so that the kitchen Sister you clothed may come back, and you will bring her here.1 About sending those to Ovada, I wrote to the Father.

  2. It will be good to keep the postulants' dormitory, the upstairs one, clean and well prepared, so that when the postulants come they find their beds; only the sheets should be missing, since they will bring their own, as is well known.

  3. That person will tell you how to say something to Corina and Eufrasina, or else he can do it with you present, as though it came from you.2

  4. My dear Adelaide, blessed daughter, courage, we shall soon see each other; I shall be in Foligno and you will sleep there, and in the morning we shall leave for Rome. But be strong, for charity's sake. Are you pleased with the Religious I chose for you? Leave the keys with that person;3 put the guest-quarters key and the little room key in the cupboard. Likewise the chapter room, the large wardrobe, the church: lock them all and then give the key to [that] person; give him two: one for the

cupboard and the other for the little room. Be sure to bring money, orange-flower water and some chicken to eat on the journey; I have had no more letters from you, but I hope you are better and have done what I wrote.4

Goodbye, my dear; the Lord bless you, and believe me always your

Affectionate Mother

5. The Parish Priest wrote to me that in a few days Gaudenzi will collect the money.5 I am telling you to bring some here too, as it comes to 3500; you can bring 1500 -; for charity's sake don't lose it.

She hopes she has received the letters and the application to submit to the Superintendent of Studies. She will send her two postulants; she is to nurture them with the other two. She should have prayers said. What she said about the accounts is fine.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Now I am answering your two letters myself, and I tell you that you have done everything well; I hope by now you have received the two Sr. A. Vincenza wrote you, [one] of which enclosed the application to submit to the Superintendent of Studies.1 Let us hope Saint Anne puts everything right. As soon as you receive this, answer me at once.

  2. I shall send you two postulants: one is the sister of the one who, so to speak, together gave the house in Foligno, and she is the elder; treat her as a postulant.2 I won't describe her character, for you will see it; the other is from here in Rome, or rather was living here, placed with me by a religious to whom I am under obligation.3 The reason I am sending them I cannot tell you here in a letter. Put the two of them, indeed three (and four) with the one you have accepted; so with Maddalena there are four.4

  3. This young lady is not very strong; you can put her in the school or wherever you think best, but never send her to the sick with the old one, unless the old one

asks you, and even then don't trust her, for she talks too much. If by chance there came... for charity's sake, enough.5 I shall write more clearly by other means, for I always fear letters get lost. So see that they become good and I shall soon take them.

4. I am pleased about the adoration. Yes, my dear, pray and have others pray a great deal.

5. The accounts are fine, and I hope you will be able to settle everything. Meanwhile I have written about Sr. A. Giovanna, so that what you wrote to me about may be sent to you to obtain the 100 F.;6 as for the Albarelli money, write to the Superior Adelaide and find out where you must go to be paid. If need be, I shall write to Signora lussi in Bologna,7 since you will need this too.

6. I await at once a letter from you saying you have received this and understood all I wrote; then I shall telegraph you when to fetch them from the station.

The Lord bless you all, while I remain your

Affectionate Mother

She sends him some pictures of Saint Anne and the outline of the Institute.

Most Reverend Excellency,

1. I take the liberty of sending you some pictures of Saint Anne together with the outline of our poor Institute, asking at the same time for your Apostolic blessing, in the hope of receiving it again in Veroli, in Your Excellency's Diocese.1

Humbly I remain, with the deepest veneration, Your Most Reverend Excellency's

Most humble Sr. Anna M. R. G.

notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc1: I have your letter: undated, but surely of the 25th, the day after the Mother's departure. She tells her of Fr Tornatore's visit and of the report she had given him about the improper behaviour of some Sisters. I am sorry ... he is going to the country. In the summer months the Lazarists of the Alberoni College went to their estate at Veano (PC).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc2: She had set a monthly fee of 15 francs and 50 on entry.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc3: Sr. A. Francesca had written to her: "...I did not receive Communion; the reason is that I am so cold that I say: it will be better not to. Mother, write me something, comfort me with a line from you". The "consolation" she asked for is given with such gentleness and wisdom as to free her from all doubt, fear and coldness.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc4: Sr. A. Francesca reassures her: everything she had given him had been returned. She also tells her of the dinner Gigino had wanted to give some friends in the House's guest quarters: the parents and two brothers of Don Gaetano Bersano, the son of Secretary Merli, two Piacenza schoolmasters and two others.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc5: The sister to be handed over to her parents is Sr. A. Cristina Carrara; for health reasons she was being sent home.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc6: It is of the day before. She reported that Fr Tornatore, having gone to visit the Marchioness Marianna Anguissola to try to persuade her to give a substantial gift to the House of Saint Anne (at least 3,000 francs were needed), had been mortified by her refusal.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc7: There is not enough information to understand what the Mother meant here.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc8: Sr. A. Eufemia Mirisola was ill in the House in Via della Morte.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc9: Thursday: 29 August. The letter for that person, cf. L 287, 5.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc10: Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti had been transferred from Sampierdarena to Piacenza, Mother House.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc11: Sr. A. Paola herself, no longer being Superior, was supposed to hand in and receive outgoing and incoming letters open (as was then the custom).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc12: The two sisters had spoken inappropriately about the problems of women who were pregnant. Cf. L of Sr. A. Francesca of 26.8.72.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc13: Having been in Ferrara for three days, she was going to pay her respects to His Eminence Cardinal Luigi Vannicelli.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc17: The letter is dated 27 August. Signor Giuseppe Defilippi, of the Vincentian Fathers at the Alberoni College and confessor of the community in Via della Morte, had told her that Sr. A. Eufemia had no confidence in the community's doctor (Sante Albertazzi) and that he had suggested the doctor of the Alberoni College to her. Sr. A. Francesca had replied that this was not permissible without informing the Mother.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc19: Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti, Sr. A. Pia Cipollini.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc20:
The girls had "dirtied the wall of the little rooms". The Superior had not managed to find out who did it. And since she feared they would go on daubing — she had indeed found "black powder hidden behind the door" — she asked the Mother for effective advice. The Mother suggests it: let them apologize with humility; and finally let a good (= timely and effective)

scolding be given.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc21: Fr Tornatore had pointed out to her that she was sometimes unable to carry out her task of warning and correcting a Sister while remaining calm and at peace. In reporting it to the Mother, Sr. A. Francesca appears somewhat resentful.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc22: Cristina Carrara (cf. L 288, n. 1) left on the morning of the 28th (cf. L of Francesca Camisa to Mother Rosa of 28.8.72).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc23: She refers to what is said in note 1. Tomorrow: Thursday 29 August.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc24: ...from the country, from Veano (cf. L 287, n. 1).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc25: Sr. A. Adelaide's letter is missing, and it is impossible to tell even from other sources what this paragraph is about regarding Mgr Mariano Wanstienkist and the persons named.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc26: The Mother held to very different principles and cannot hide her sorrow.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc27: "...keep silent with Ninetta". Signora Anna Costa, widow Bergami, confidante, friend and secretary of Countess Maria Anna Trotti. Great prudence was needed in speaking with her, because she reported everything to the Countess. The Sisters certainly had reason to complain. Being inconstant and of a fickle, strange character, she helped the Sisters only occasionally with a gift, while on the other hand the people of Ferrara gave them no alms, believing the Countess supported them.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc28:
I pray... troubles and sorrows: this is the response to Jesus' Gospel command: pray for your persecutors (Mt 5:44), extended to the subtle forms of "troubles and sorrows" certainly not caused by goodwill and friendship. ...in this way we are sure:

we are sure of being and behaving as "daughters of the heavenly Father" (Mt 5:45).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc29:
This paragraph is full of the Gospel spirit. Starting from the Beatitudes, the Mother leads her daughter along the way of "suffering" that leads to "eternal joy". Cf.

Mt 5:10; Rom 8:35; 1 Pet 2:19; 3:14; 4:14, etc.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc30: ...give peace to her heart. The Mother understands that the Countess's conduct stems from inner conflict, which makes her suffer and causes suffering to others. No words or advice can heal her, only prayer.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc31: Sr. A. Panasia Bellardi, as Sr. A. Adelaide's letters to M. Rosa show, had an unstable character and "wasted herself" on many "silly things". Cf. L 279, n. 1. Sr. A. Eletta Bruschi, cf. L 284, 2.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc32: Sr. A. Serafina Lorenzi, Superior of the nursing Community in Genoa, was in great suffering.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc33: A uniform for the boarders was indispensable and was regarded by outsiders as a sign of the good and orderly running of any institution worthy of consideration and respect. Some mothers had already complained of its absence.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc35: She wants the Mother to write and the Mother obliges, but with pain, having seen for herself how she reacts to correction: she takes offence, makes "scenes", is overcome by "a thousand ailments". After this introduction she speaks of the pain she felt seeing her "ever more irritable", "raising her voice", complaining that "they're all interested in whether she has money or not", and then her nervous tension; and further: "To hide from the Sisters that we are poor"! Sr. A. Adelaide accepts the corrections: "Everything you say is true... I assure you I did not realize it was wrong; now that you have warned me so kindly, I promise to be more careful... I am deeply sorry to have caused you displeasure..." (Cf. L to M. Rosa of 5.9.72).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc36: The letter to the Sisters follows here, paragraphs 7-13.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc37: The "daughter" thanks her for opening her eyes, promises not to lose her temper, and concludes: "I put myself in your hands, do with me as you will... pray that Saint Anne may make me her true Daughter" (ibid.).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc39: Cf. Lettere 1, p. 524. She had died on 22 October 1871.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc40: Through inadvertence she dated it from Piacenza instead of Genoa, where she certainly was, as the correspondence of the day before and the day after shows.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc41: The first is Adelaide Campidelli, who entered the house at Sampierdarena; the second, Piralli Angela. AFSA Reg. Postulants nos. 144 and 150.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc42: She charges her to ask Giuseppe Brigidini for the 700 francs raised by a lottery then under way for the benefit of the Mother House, he being in charge of organizing it (Cf. Brigidini's letters to Sr. A. Francesca AFSA, F 24, 4).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc43:
The Marchioness is certainly Marianna Anguissola, but after the verb "will"

the object is missing. The Mother foresees that she will turn a deaf ear, as at other times, and so ends with an act of trust in God.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc44: Sr. A. Francesca sometimes complained of friction among the Sisters of the Community in Via della Morte. One of them was Sr. A. Fortunata Zucconi, long ill. Cf. L 182, n. 2.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc47: Sr. A. Maddalena Terzaghi, cf. AFSA, D 2, 5.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc49: This letter was catalogued under the date 16 August 1872; in fact it does not belong to that time, first because the Mother was ill in Piacenza and also because of its content, which refers to situations clearly matching the date given here. Moreover, on close inspection of the date in the original one can see that the 1 before the 6 is actually a stroke and the month that at first sight looks like 8 is actually 9. Mother Rosa, as is known, usually wrote in haste; and this letter in particular is telegraphic.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc50: Giuseppe Squarzoni was Countess Maria Anna Trotti's steward in Ferrara.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc51: The Mother has learned that the Countess has decided to give 1,000 francs; she seeks, however, a way to urge the steward to hand them over, and at the same time excuses him "for his immense occupations".
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc52: Once again the Superior had told the Mother: Sr. A. Panasia yesterday began her usual weeping. Cf. L 279, n. 1.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc53: The Sisters had made a number of insoles for a Jewish merchant, and also several shirts. This was the way of providence, in the absence of alms. So she urges her to look for other work, relying on the religious of the city, who knew the merchants, or at any rate anyone who could commission sewing and embroidery from them.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc54: Work continued in the Chapel and the house, though slowly.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc55: Clearly, after receiving the money she was to thank the Countess by letter.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc56: The Superior is the good Sr. A. Serafina Lorenzi, long in poor health.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc57: When you go. At the beginning of September, by the Mother's wish, the Superior had been moved to the House at Sampierdarena, better suited to her condition both for the better air and for convenience. Sr. A. Santina was standing in for the Superior in the Genoa Community.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc58:
Sr. A. Adelaide had written to her on 14 September: "Today at 2 p.m.

the Caracciolo (Countess Isabella) turned up unexpectedly with her two brothers (Francesco and Maurizio) and Fr Cirillo". On the last, cf. L 180, n. 5.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc59: ...have a lesson. Nursing instruction given to the Sisters by the Superior was normal practice. Cf. Application of the Common Rules of the Delegate, n. 21.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc61: In the letter mentioned above, Adelaide had told her that Countess Isabella had been surprised to see in the Chapel the picture of Saint Anne that had belonged to her mother, for she was convinced it was in Piacenza in the House in Via della Morte. Now the Mother writes that she will explain to Countess Isabella that the picture is in Ferrara provisionally, until Countess Trotti has donated her own.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc64: The Ursuline Sisters had invited the Superior "to the solemn prize-giving".
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc69: A certain canon of Ferrara, whose name Sr. A. Adelaide says she has forgotten, had composed a song in honour of Countess Maria Anna Trotti and wanted a music master to teach it to the day pupils. (Cf. L Sr. A. Adelaide to Mother Rosa 10.9.1872).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc71: The Sisters embroidering it had told the Superior Adelaide that it would be ready on the 18th (cf. L Adelaide to M. Rosa 14.9.1872).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc72: I hear about Squarzoni... The Countess's steward had not yet handed over the thousand francs offered by the Countess, who writes her many things, shows herself favourable and promises help, but meanwhile the alterations to the House are suspended. So she urges Sr. A. Adelaide to call on Squarzoni often, also because he is to give her a clock.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc73: ...Sr. A. Camilla Bonetti. Sr. A. Adelaide assures her she is gradually persuading her to be punctual in Chapel for meditation. (L Adelaide Pezzoni to M. Rosa, 12.9.1872).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc75: The Sisters, long ill in the infirmary House in Via della Morte, Piacenza, are: Sr. A. Elena Ferrari, who died on the 19th; Sr. A. Fortunata Zucconi, Sr. A. Eufemia Mirisola and Raffaela Cordarli were quite seriously ill.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc76: In the House mentioned in the previous note the Superior is Sr. A. Filippina Bruschi.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc77: Fr Tornatore was called upon by the Sisters of Charity not only as confessor. After Siena, where the Sisters of Charity have an important work, he was to go to another of their communities at Foligno, where we shall soon open a House.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc78: ...I am delighted. The expression is significant. Cf. L 297, 2.3.7.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc79: The Mother had decided to transfer Sr. A. Giacomina Schenardi from Nizza to the Mother House, so that she ceased to serve as Superior.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc80: Fr Giuseppe Defilippi, Lazarist, confessor to the Sisters; professor at the Alberoni College.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc81: The Marchioness Marianna Anguissola; Fr Cirillo: cf. L 180, n. 5; ...to Brigidini: cf. L 293, n. 2. Condiviola was the "baker" to whom they also had a debt to pay.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc82: That is: she was able to get only a little money compared with what she had hoped for. She does not send it because she is awaiting Brigidini's reply; if he gives nothing, she will send it later. But she hopes Brigidini will give her the money from the lottery.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc83: She is worried about Sr. A. Serafina, as no improvement is to be seen.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc84: Sr. A. del Buon Pastore Bastia was unwell. To the Superior, who had asked how she could ease her situation, she replies that it would be better to move her to the infirmary (House in Via della Morte).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc85: Sr. A. Giacomina could take on the office of sacristan, but only if Sr. A. del Buon Pastore became seriously ill; otherwise it is better to say nothing to her.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc86:
The postulant: Torielli Maria; I would like her to stay... she had been presented and warmly recommended by Don Luigi Milano, who had worked hard for the FSA to go to Nizza. Cf. L to M. Rosa of 6.12.1871, AFSA.

Lay Letters.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc87: You will talk to the Parish Priest of Settima. He was to handle the sale of the share of the inheritance of Sr. A. Emilia Dedamo, of Settima (PC).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc88: Sr. A. Eufemia Mirisola was ill. Sr. A. Francesca had told the Mother (L 19.9.1872) that she would ask the attending doctor to prescribe another treatment.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc89:
...the deed of division: see note 10 above. The Secretary: Signor Merli.

In short, I put. A Genoese expression. In short, I have set so many initiatives going that I hope to obtain a good result.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc91: She had arrived in Nice on the 23rd; the 25th is presumed for two reasons: the content relating to events, and the following letters, from the 26th on, all properly dated.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc92: Cf. L 300, n. 2. Call her Sr. A. Giacomina: without the title Superior, because she no longer held that office.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc93: Cf. L 300, n. 4. To Sr. A. Pia Cipollini.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc94: tell her: tell the Superior Filippina (Bruschi) that I will write to her.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc95: Trust... everything will be resolved and she will be able to pay the large debts. Cf. L 300, n. 12.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc96:
...your letter: of 24 September. The Sisters are well, except one;

Squarzoni came to the House but did not bring her the Countess's money. The Mother is referring to this news.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc97:
The Superior Serafina (cf. L 291, n. 8) is ill, but she cannot move;

she will leave on the 30th and arrive in Genoa at midnight.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc98:
...tell Giovanna Bixio. This Sister — writes Adelaide in the letter cited — finding herself before a mirror in a patient's house, "saw her reflection, came home terrified, lost heart and says she has not long to live".

Sr. A. Giovanna was 56. The Mother gives her a good shake. She has work to do in a hospital that is to be opened.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc99:
In the same letter the Superior had written: "We owe the priest L.

120; I am ashamed; he always stares at me; his eyes seem to say: you don't pay me".

The Mother advises her to look for a priest who will celebrate Mass free of charge.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc100:
Sr. A. Francesca's letter is of 28 September 1872; I hear what you say about providence: "Mother, providence is always scarce"; the Priests who came: "Rev. Luigi Malfina, Vicar of Soresina, sent by Countess Primoli"

came to ask for news of her...; and Fr Defilippi.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc101: Sr. A. Giacomina Schenardi is to be house nurse and to nurse the sick in their homes. Cf. L 300, n. 2.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc102: ...Ten manuals of Saint Anne, cf. L 131, n. 2, to Canon Tommaso Quasso.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc104: Cf. L 180, n. 5. She wrote asking him to speak of the House's need to a wealthy family he knew.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc106: Cf. L 300, 3; ...the one you put to sleep downstairs. She is the postulant from Acqui: cf. L 300, 6 and its note.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc107: She feels her sorrows and makes them her own, taking them on inwardly, but she cannot exempt her from the law of suffering. From trial accepted with firmness — you must be strong — springs God's consolation.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc108: Courage... console you. Here is one of the teachings so frequent in M. Rosa's letters to her Daughters. Courage!: it is fortitude kept awake and strengthened by hope: good Jesus will come to console you. Alas, we have experienced how frail men are; they have nothing for us but crosses and sorrows.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc109:
She now comes down to two causes of suffering:

- The Countess has asked for the wardrobe in which the Sisters keep the linen. The Mother finds the solution, taking the drama out of it and making it a cause for mirth. That is how they must behave in everything.

- Daily Mass at home is impossible because of the expense, which the community cannot bear. There is a remedy: ask Mgr Luigi Giordani, the Bishop.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc110: Finally, the infallible remedy: faith and trust in God and the promise of his unfailing faithfulness: you will see that He will set everything right.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc113: On Friday the 27th the doctors had seen the possibility of recovery.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc115: Fr Tornatore had gone to Siena and then to Foligno to preach the Spiritual Exercises to the Daughters of Charity. Cf. L 299, 5.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc116: The date is inferred from the context.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc117: From the letters of Sr. A. Serafina, Superior of the Genoa house, to M. Rosa it appears that the Sisters had nursed Signora Biale on several occasions. On 21.9.1872 she writes: "We still go to Signora Biale; now she is ill; she has received viaticum" (cf. AFSA, D 1). Don Giovanni Biale is surely the deceased's brother.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc118: If they iron: if they iron the albs, they should not starch them, because the lace has to be put on.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc120: Place and date are inferred from the context.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc121:
The Mother wanted to transfer Sr. A. Prassede Croce and Sr. A.

Luduina Delfini to the Mother House for their unexemplary conduct. So she explains to the Superior how to proceed. Give Sr. A. Prassede humble work, and if she pleads reasons of health, tell her plainly that the sick are cared for in the infirmary in Via della Morte. And let her be clear and firm in threatening both with dismissal from the Institute if they speak about what happens in the Houses they come from (the ones you came from).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc122: Fr Giuseppe Manfredini SJ had preached the Spiritual Exercises to the community of the Mother House. Cf. L 161, n. 1.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc123: Polleri bequest. Established in Genoa and administered there by a Commission.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc124: Sr. A. Francesca had written to her on 30 April that the providence of nursing the sick never fails, "but it would be good if it came from elsewhere".
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc125: The postulant accepted: Piralli Angela, presented by the Parish Priest of Varallo, Don Giuseppe Neri. AFSA, Register of Postulants, no. 150. Cf. L 303, 5.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc127:
She has changed her mind about the decision in note 2. The reason?

Scarcity, given the serious want.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc128: In her letter (of 30 September) Sr. A. Francesca had, however, reassured her: "It's nothing much". She had long been diagnosed with chronic tracheitis.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc129: The date is inferred from the context.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc131: Don Antonio Accinelli. A friend of the Gattorno family, he looked after M. Rosa's financial interests concerning her family. He also followed the first communities founded in Liguria and Piedmont, especially the financial soundness of those of Genoa and Sampierdarena.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc132: ...the reduced-fare railway tickets she had requested and obtained from the Piacenza stationmaster. ...Sr. A. Nazzarena Pastorini was in charge of the kitchen; the other, probably Sr. A. Giovannina, was her assistant.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc133: ...your letters: two of 30 September, one of 2 October, in which she reports on the people (Sisters, postulants, girls), the critical financial situation and her own conduct.
